entry.title: This is my brain on Julia…

link.title: This is my brain on Julia…

entry.content:
A few months back my company prototyped one of our bidding projects in Julia to try and address performance issues with the current python implementation. That project didnt end up panning out, but what I saw of Julia impressed me. A staticly typed, compiled language, with the rich type inference and dead simple syntax of python? Native support for Nd matrices - speed comparable to numpy or c/++? Nice!

Pros

So far, I’ve been really happy working with Julia, especially compared to any other staticly typed, compiled language I worked with. Setup was a breeze - and the vscode extension is amazing. Julia works seamlessly with vscode’s jupyter tooling and the linting worked out of the box for me. Except for Python, Julia has easily has the best Jupyter support of any language I’ve worked with. Error messages are clear and to the point, the package manager is great, and the syntax is super simple and concise, comparable to python or go.

I think what I like most about Julia is that I really think I can do anything with it. If I want to treat it as a scripting language like js or python, I can quickly type out the functionality I want. If I want to use it for scientific computing, the ecosystem is there and comparable to something like Matlab (w/o the exorbitant cost). But, when it comes time to write more serious production code, I have the tools to optimize it and (importantly) get speedups from multithreading.

Cons

Unfortunately Julia also has its flaws. Its primarily a scientific computing language - AFAIK there are no large companies who use Julia as a core part of their stack.

Syntactically speaking - the 1-based indexing is a bizarre choice and I find myself subtracting 1 from many index vars just to emulate 0-indexing - but given Julia is a scientific language it kindof makes sense that it would inherit some traits from Matlab. While I enjoy being able to define blocks and capture their end value w/ begin...end and being able to control scope w/ let...end, I dont like having type out multi character keywords all the time. I also think they interfere w/ the readability of the code if I follow patterns Im used to in javascript or c++. I miss the i++ and ++i operators - the equivalent block to i++ in julia is basically unusable: begin tmp = i; i += 1; tmp end.

I also find the OO elements of Julia a little clunky. Sometimes I want objects w/ member methods that have access to data scoped to that object. You can techincally use the JS function == object == class approach in Julia - but its clunky, the syntax is unintuitive, and linting doesnt work.

Heap = () -> begin
    size = 0
    li = (n) -> 2*n + 0
    ri = (n) -> 2*n + 1
    pi = (n) -> floor(Int,n/2)
    return () -> (size;li;ri;pi)
end
o = Heap()
("o.size",o.size,"o.li(1)",o.li(1),"o.ri(1)",o.ri(1),"o.pi(1)",o.pi(1))

("o.size", 0, "o.li(1)", 2, "o.ri(1)", 3, "o.pi(1)", 0)

You can do something similar w/ classes having functions as member variables, but again, linting doesnt work and I get the feeling this just isnt how you are supposed to write Julia.

Verdict

A lot of companies use python for data engineering and datascience, and a more performant language like Java or Go for their backend. Or they might use python for ML/datascience, and Java for their pipeline and backend. Some companies even use python or JS/TS for their backend services, trading performance for ease-of-use.

I think Julia has the potential to satisfy all backend requirements w/o the need for tradeoffs. AFAICT it has good performance and good support for threading. I see a lot of the packages and connectors you might need for data & app engineeering (DB, ORM, kafka, spark, AWS sdk, etc…) - and Julia of course satisfies any datascience or ML need.

BUT - Julia just isnt as common as the industry standards and doesnt have the backing of any large company. Coming from python, comparable packages in Julia arent as mature as you might like (this was the main reason my company decided not continue down the Julia path).

Overall? Id like to use Julia, and will continue to advocate it for backend tasks when possible - but I just dont see any manager agreeing. Bummer :/

… a few weeks later …

Oh right - wasnt this post supposed to be about RSA? Well - I dont want this one getting too long - and I really dont want a half finished post up for another month. So Im splitting it here - au revoir loyal readers!

entry.title: This is my brain…
entry.content:
I recently - well - not that recently (about a year ago) - switched from a job where I worked 60+ hr weeks to one where I work a standard 40 hours. Since the company is EST and I live in PST, Im basically free after 2pm. Now that I have some time on my hands, Ive been taking my hobby projects a little more seriously. I’ve also brought some of my old projects back from the dead and given them a little facelift - namely my old Starcraft bot. Anyways - I think the time has come to start writing up some of these projects and showing them off.

I think Ill start by posting a quick writeup I did on my first experiences w/ the Julia language using it to code out an implementation of RSA from scratch. I will say - as I was writing that post - I found it getting a little long and unfocused. Does a reader really want to see my fumbling attempts at showing why optimizations like Carmichaels totient and the Chinese remainder theorem are useful and important? Is it really useful to explain Miller-Rabin? I think I might have to cut it down and may just focus on the basics of the algo and its goals. We’ll see.

I think next I’ll probably write up something on using powerful ML estimators like Xgboost or sklearns MLP implementation as a Kaplan Meier estimator for survival analysis. Its a problem that comes up surprisingly often, and I’ve found the already implemented algorithms in the excellent liflines package are too slow for the kind of rich datasets you encounter in a professional context.

After that …. I’m not sure. I made a fun little AI for the popular 2048 game to beat my brother’s high score. I think I finally understand alpha/beta pruning now - as well as the importance of a good hueristic function and why OpenAI used machine learning for their hueristics. Also I think an a post w/ an embedded widget of my AI autoplaying the game would be cool.

I also spent a lot of time working on a VR physics/animation engine for Babylon.js for an Avatar game. That project needs a ton of work though, and I actually had to stop working on it for a bit b/c I ran into a version conflict b/w the packages I was using. I’ll probably come back to it later, but to be honest I dont know when I could demo it on this blog.

I might write up an analysis of CDC vaccination and VAERS data I did after a discussion w/ a couple friends where I realized that it was difficult to find any objective hard analyses of effect size online. I do worry that by the time I get around to that writeup Ill have to redo all the work to stay up to date.

I may also revisit a topic I researched in college and have returned to off and on ever since. Every year EIA and Lazard publish LCOE #s for various power sources, and whenever they are discussed online I see a lot of confusion about how the numbers are calcuated and what they mean. I also see people posting a lot of #s from source specific orgs like IRENA and IAEA, and making all kinds of apples to oranges comparisons. I think I could do a ton of posts about either one of those topics, but I might just start out w/ a replication of LCOE #s and some discussion about input parameters and assumptions.

Well - I think thats all I have for the forseeable future — looking forward to what I can get done by EOY.
